q: What is the S.I. unit of electric charge? (JAC 2020, 2021)
e: The S.I. unit of electric charge is the coulomb (symbol C).

q: What is the S.I. unit of electric current? (JAC 2020)
e: The S.I. unit of electric current (I = Q/t) is the ampere (A).

q: What is the S.I. unit of electric potential difference?
e: Potential difference (V = W/Q) has the S.I. unit volt (V = 1 J/C).

q: What is the S.I. unit of electrical resistance? (JAC 2020, 2024)
e: Electrical resistance (R = V/I) is measured in ohm (Ω).

q: What is the S.I. unit of electric power?
e: The S.I. unit of electric power is the watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s = 1 V·A.

q: What is the S.I. unit of electrical resistivity (ρ)?
e: From ρ = R·A/l, the S.I. unit of resistivity is ohm-metre (Ω·m).

q: Which instrument measures electric current in a circuit, and how is it connected? (JAC 2021)
e: An ammeter measures electric current and is always connected in series.

q: Name the instrument used to measure potential difference across two points and its mode of connection.
e: A voltmeter measures potential difference and is connected in parallel across the component.

q: 1 kilowatt-hour (1 kWh), the commercial unit of electrical energy, is equal to how many joules?
Approximately how many electrons make up 1 coulomb (1 C) of electric charge? (NCERT)
e: Using Q = ne: n = 1 / (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 6.25 × 10¹⁸ electrons.

q: What is the magnitude of charge on a single electron?
e: Each electron carries an elementary charge of magnitude 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

q: Which metal is used almost exclusively for making the filament of an electric incandescent bulb? (JAC 2024)
e: Tungsten has an extremely high melting point (3380°C), allowing it to glow white-hot without melting.

q: Which chemically inactive gases are filled inside electric bulbs to prolong the life of the filament?
e: Chemically unreactive nitrogen and argon gases prevent oxidation of the hot tungsten filament.

q: Why are heating elements of electric toasters and irons made of an alloy (such as nichrome) rather than a pure metal?
o: Alloys have high resistivity and do not oxidise (burn) readily at high temperatures
e: Nichrome combines high electrical resistivity with strong resistance to oxidation even when red hot.

q: Which of the following terms does NOT represent electrical power in a circuit? (NCERT / JAC 2026)
e: Electric power equals VI, I²R, or V²/R; IR² does not represent power.

q: According to Ohm's law at constant temperature, what is the relation between potential difference V and current I? (JAC 2020, 2021)
e: Ohm's law states that at constant temperature, V ∝ I, giving V/I = R or V = IR.

q: What is the shape of the V–I graph for a metallic conductor obeying Ohm's law?
o: A straight line passing through the origin
A line parallel to the X-axis
e: Since V is directly proportional to I, the V–I graph is a straight line through the origin.

q: Which device is used to regulate current by changing resistance in a circuit without changing the voltage source?
e: A rheostat acts as a variable resistor to adjust circuit current without altering source voltage.

q: 1 Horse Power (HP) is equal to how many watts?
e: One mechanical horsepower (1 HP) equals 746 watts.

q: An electric fuse wire is commonly made of an alloy of which metals?
e: Lead–tin solder alloy has a suitable low melting point, melting quickly to break overloaded circuits.

q: Which substance is the best conductor of electricity (having the lowest resistivity)?
e: Silver has the lowest electrical resistivity (1.60 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m) and is the best conductor.

q: If resistors R₁, R₂ and R₃ are connected in series, what is their equivalent resistance R_s?
e: In series combination, the equivalent resistance equals the sum of individual resistances: R₁ + R₂ + R₃.

q: If two resistors R₁ and R₂ are connected in parallel, what is the formula for equivalent resistance R_p?
e: In parallel, the reciprocal of equivalent resistance equals the sum of reciprocals: 1/R_p = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂.

q: What is the correct mathematical expression for Joule's law of heating?
e: According to Joule's law of heating, heat produced in a resistor is H = I²Rt.

q: What is taken as the direction of conventional electric current in a metallic circuit?
o: Along the flow of electrons (negative to positive)
Opposite to electron flow (from positive terminal to negative terminal)
e: By convention, current flows from positive to negative terminal, opposite to the flow of negative electrons.

q: What kind of physical quantity is electric potential?
e: Both work and charge are scalars, making electric potential a scalar quantity.

q: How does the resistance R of a uniform metallic conductor depend on its length l and cross-sectional area A?
e: Resistance is directly proportional to length l and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area A: R = ρ(l/A).

q: Which of the following does the resistivity (ρ) of a conductor depend upon? (JAC 2025)
o: Nature of the material and temperature
e: Resistivity ρ is an intrinsic property of a material; it depends on the material's nature and temperature, not shape or dimensions.

q: In what arrangement are household appliances connected in domestic electric circuits?
e: Domestic circuits wire appliances in parallel so every device gets full 220 V and can be switched independently.

q: What should be the resistance of an ideal or practical ammeter so it does not alter circuit current?
e: Since an ammeter sits in series, it must have very low (ideally zero) resistance to avoid dropping current.

q: 1 milliampere (1 mA) and 1 microampere (1 μA) respectively equal:
e: 1 mA = 10⁻³ A and 1 μA = 10⁻⁶ A.

q: Three resistors of 2 Ω, 4 Ω, and 6 Ω are connected in series. What is their equivalent resistance? (JAC 2021)
e: In series, R_s = 2 + 4 + 6 = 12 Ω.

q: What is the minimum resistance that can be made using five resistors each of 1/5 Ω? (JAC 2025 / NCERT Exemplar)
e: Minimum resistance comes from parallel combination: R_min = R/n = (1/5)/5 = 1/25 Ω.

q: What is the maximum resistance obtainable using five resistors each of 1/5 Ω?
e: Maximum resistance comes from series combination: R_max = 5 × (1/5 Ω) = 1 Ω.

q: A metallic conductor has resistivity ρ. If its shape is bent or its length is changed at constant temperature, what happens to its resistivity ρ? (JAC 2025)
e: Resistance changes with geometry, but resistivity ρ depends only on the material and temperature, so it stays unchanged.

q: If a wire of resistance R is stretched to double its original length (halving its cross-sectional area), what becomes its new resistance?
e: With length doubled (2l) and area halved (A/2), R' = ρ(2l)/(A/2) = 4R.

q: Why are copper and aluminium wires usually employed for electricity transmission? (NCERT)
o: They have the lowest melting points
They have very low resistivity, minimising energy loss as heat
e: Low resistivity of copper and aluminium minimises resistive heating losses over long transmission distances.

q: Which statements highlight the advantages of connecting electrical appliances in parallel instead of series?
o: Equivalent resistance decreases, each gets full supply voltage, and devices switch independently
Same current flows through every load regardless of power
Failure of one appliance switches off all others
e: Parallel wiring lowers total resistance, delivers full voltage to each load, and allows independent control.

q: When R₁ = 3 Ω and R₂ = 6 Ω are connected in parallel, what is the equivalent resistance and how does it compare?
o: 2 Ω (even smaller than the smallest 3 Ω resistor)
e: 1/R_p = 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2 => R_p = 2 Ω, which is always smaller than the smallest individual resistance.

q: In a circuit, an electric fuse is connected in which mode and with which wire?
o: In series with the live wire
e: A fuse is placed in series with the live wire so excessive current cuts off high-voltage supply immediately.

q: What are the common standard current ratings of domestic fuses in India (per NCERT)?
o: 1 A, 2 A, 3 A, 5 A, 10 A (and 15 A for heavy appliances)
e: Per NCERT, domestic fuses carry standard ratings such as 1 A, 2 A, 3 A, 5 A, 10 A (plus 15 A for heavy-power lines).

q: If the current flowing through a fixed resistor is doubled for the same time interval, how does the heat generated change?
e: Since H = I²Rt, doubling current increases heat by 2² = 4 times.

q: Why must a voltmeter have an extremely high (ideally infinite) resistance?
o: So all circuit current passes through it
So it draws negligible current when placed in parallel and reads true potential difference
e: High resistance ensures negligible current bypasses into the voltmeter, preserving the true potential difference.

q: Which statement is true for unequal resistors R₁ and R₂ connected in series across a battery?
o: Potential difference across both is equal
The exact same current flows through both, while potential difference divides proportionally (V ∝ R)
Larger resistor has smaller voltage drop
e: A single series path forces equal current I through every resistor, splitting voltage as V₁:V₂ = R₁:R₂.

q: For two unequal resistors R₁ < R₂ connected in parallel across a battery, which statement is true?
o: Both have the same potential difference, and larger current flows through smaller resistance R₁
e: Parallel branches share the same voltage V, so I = V/R gives greater current in the smaller resistor.

q: What is the primary function of an electric cell or battery in a circuit?
o: Convert chemical energy to maintain a potential difference across the circuit terminals
e: Chemical reactions inside a cell maintain a potential difference across its terminals that drives current.

q: If a uniform wire is cut into 3 equal pieces, what happens to the resistivity (ρ) of each piece?
o: Resistivity stays unchanged (ρ), while each piece's resistance drops to R/3
e: Resistivity is an intrinsic material constant (stays ρ), whereas resistance is proportional to length (drops to R/3).

q: In a V–I graph with V plotted on the Y-axis and I on the X-axis, what does the slope of the line (ΔV/ΔI) represent?
e: With V on the vertical axis and I on the horizontal axis, slope ΔV/ΔI equals resistance R.

q: Watch the axes: if a graph plots current I on the Y-axis against voltage V on the X-axis, what does the slope (ΔI/ΔV) represent?
e: Here slope = I/V = 1/R, so a steeper I–V line corresponds to a smaller resistance.

q: Which set lists ONLY appliances that work primarily on the heating effect of electric current?
o: Electric iron, toaster, water heater (and fuse)
e: Electric irons, toasters, geysers, kettles, filament bulbs, and electric fuses rely on Joule heating.

q: An electric bulb is rated 220 V and 100 W. When it is operated on 110 V, the power consumed will be: (NCERT)
e: Bulb resistance R = 220²/100 = 484 Ω. At 110 V (half voltage), P' = 110²/484 = 25 W.

q: What is the correct increasing order of electrical resistivity among pure metals, alloys, and insulators?
o: Pure metals (~10⁻⁸ Ω·m) < Alloys (~10⁻⁶ Ω·m) < Insulators (~10¹²–10¹⁷ Ω·m)
e: Pure metals (~10⁻⁸ Ω·m) have the lowest resistivity, followed by alloys (~10⁻⁶ Ω·m), while insulators reach 10¹²–10¹⁷ Ω·m.

q: If the diameter of a metallic wire is halved while keeping its length and material unchanged, what happens to its resistance?
e: Since A = πd²/4, halving diameter quarters cross-sectional area, multiplying resistance by 4.

q: What is the physical meaning of a closed switch versus an open switch in an electric circuit?
o: Closed switch stops current; open switch flows current
Closed switch completes the path so current flows; open switch breaks the path so current stops
e: A closed plug key/switch bridges the gap to allow current; an open switch interrupts the circuit.

q: How is 1 volt (1 V) of potential difference defined? (NCERT)
o: Potential difference is 1 V if 1 joule of work is done in moving 1 coulomb of charge from one point to the other
e: From V = W/Q, 1 volt equals 1 joule of work per 1 coulomb of charge (1 J/C).

q: What happens if an ammeter is mistakenly connected in parallel across an electric bulb or battery?
o: Because of its extremely low resistance, a huge short-circuit current flows through the ammeter, likely burning/damaging it
e: An ammeter's near-zero resistance acts like a short circuit in parallel, drawing excessive current that can burn its coil.

q: What happens if a high-resistance voltmeter is accidentally connected in series in a circuit?
o: Due to its huge resistance, circuit current drops nearly to zero and the load will not work
e: Inserting a voltmeter's megaohm resistance in series restricts current virtually to zero.

q: An electric oven of 2 kW power rating is operated in a domestic 220 V circuit having a current rating of 5 A. What result do you expect? (JAC 2020 / NCERT)
o: The oven draws I = 2000/220 ≈ 9.09 A (> 5 A), causing overloading and blowing the circuit fuse
e: I = P/V = 2000/220 ≈ 9.09 A exceeds the 5 A circuit rating, overloading the line and blowing the fuse.

q: How much current will an electric bulb draw from a 220 V source if the resistance of the bulb filament is 1200 Ω? (NCERT Ex 12.3)
e: Using Ohm's law, I = V/R = 220 / 1200 ≈ 0.18 A.

q: Why are alloys like Constantan or Manganin preferred for making standard resistance coils?
o: Their resistance drops rapidly with temperature
They have high resistivity and negligible variation of resistance with temperature
e: These alloys combine high resistivity with minimal temperature sensitivity, keeping calibration accurate.

q: A current of 0.5 A is drawn by a filament of an electric bulb for 10 minutes. Find the amount of electric charge flowing through the circuit. (NCERT Ex 12.1)
e: Converting t = 10 min = 600 s, charge Q = I × t = 0.5 × 600 = 300 C.

q: How much work is done in moving a charge of 2 C across two points having a potential difference of 12 V? (NCERT Ex 12.2)
e: Work done W = V × Q = 12 × 2 = 24 J.

q: How much current will an electric heater coil draw from a 220 V source if the resistance of the heater coil is 100 Ω? (NCERT Ex 12.3)

The potential difference between the terminals of an electric heater is 60 V when it draws a current of 4 A. What current will it draw if the potential difference is increased to 120 V? (NCERT Ex 12.4)
e: Resistance R = 60/4 = 15 Ω. At 120 V, current I = 120/15 = 8 A.

q: A wire of given material having length l and cross-sectional area A has a resistance of 4 Ω. What would be the resistance of another wire of the same material having length l/2 and area 2A? (NCERT Ex 12.6)
An electric lamp of 20 Ω and a conductor of 4 Ω resistance are connected in series to a 6 V battery. Calculate the circuit current and potential difference across the lamp. (NCERT Ex 12.7)
e: R_total = 20 + 4 = 24 Ω => I = 6/24 = 0.25 A. Voltage across the lamp = 0.25 × 20 = 5 V.

q: Resistors R₁ = 5 Ω, R₂ = 10 Ω, and R₃ = 30 Ω are connected in parallel to a 12 V battery. Find total current and equivalent resistance. (NCERT Ex 12.8)
100 J of heat is produced each second in a 4 Ω resistance. Find the potential difference across the resistor. (NCERT Ex 12.11)
e: From H = I²Rt: 100 = I²(4)(1) => I = 5 A, so V = I·R = 5 × 4 = 20 V.

q: An electric bulb is connected to a 220 V generator. The current is 0.50 A. What is the power of the bulb? (NCERT Ex 12.12)
e: Electric power P = V × I = 220 × 0.50 = 110 W.

q: An electric refrigerator rated 400 W operates 8 hours/day. What is the cost of the energy to operate it for 30 days at Rs 3.00 per kWh? (NCERT Ex 12.13)
e: Energy = 0.4 kW × 8 h/day × 30 days = 96 kWh. Cost = 96 × ₹3 = ₹288.

q: A 6 V battery is connected in series with 5 Ω, 8 Ω, and 12 Ω resistors. What is the potential difference across the 12 Ω resistor? (JAC 2024 / NCERT)
e: R_total = 25 Ω => I = 6/25 = 0.24 A. Voltage across 12 Ω resistor = 0.24 × 12 = 2.88 V.

q: How many 176 Ω resistors (in parallel) are required to carry 5 A on a 220 V line? (NCERT)
e: Required equivalent R = 220/5 = 44 Ω. For n parallel 176 Ω resistors: 176/n = 44 => n = 4.

q: How can three resistors of resistances 2 Ω, 3 Ω, and 6 Ω be connected to give a total resistance of 4 Ω? (NCERT)
o: Connect 3 Ω and 6 Ω in parallel, then connect 2 Ω in series with them
Connect 2 Ω and 3 Ω in parallel with 6 Ω in series
e: 3 Ω || 6 Ω gives (3×6)/(3+6) = 2 Ω; adding 2 Ω in series gives 2 + 2 = 4 Ω.

q: How can 2 Ω, 3 Ω, and 6 Ω resistors be connected to obtain an equivalent resistance of 1 Ω? (NCERT)
o: Only 2 Ω and 3 Ω in parallel

q: What is (a) the highest and (b) the lowest total resistance that can be secured by combinations of four coils of 4 Ω, 8 Ω, 12 Ω, and 24 Ω? (NCERT)
e: Highest (series) = 4+8+12+24 = 48 Ω; Lowest (parallel): 1/R = (6+3+2+1)/24 = 1/2 => R_min = 2 Ω.

q: Two lamps, one rated 100 W at 220 V and the other 60 W at 220 V, are connected in parallel to a 220 V mains supply. What current is drawn from the line? (NCERT)
e: In parallel, total power is 100 + 60 = 160 W, so line current I = 160/220 ≈ 0.727 ≈ 0.73 A.

q: Which uses more energy: a 250 W TV set in 1 hour, or a 1200 W toaster in 10 minutes? (NCERT)
o: 250 W TV set uses more energy (250 Wh vs 200 Wh)
Both use the exact same energy
e: TV uses 250 × 1 = 250 Wh, while the toaster uses 1200 × (1/6) = 200 Wh. Thus the TV uses more energy.

q: An electric heater of resistance 8 Ω draws 15 A from the service mains for 2 hours. Calculate the rate at which heat is developed in the heater. (NCERT)
e: Rate of heat generation P = I²R = 15² × 8 = 225 × 8 = 1800 J/s (1800 W).

q: A piece of wire of resistance R is cut into five equal parts. These parts are then connected in parallel. If the equivalent resistance is R', what is the ratio R/R'? (NCERT)
e: Each part has resistance R/5. Connecting 5 parts in parallel gives R' = (R/5)/5 = R/25, so R/R' = 25.

q: Two conducting wires of the same material, equal lengths and equal diameters are first connected in series and then parallel across the same potential difference. Find the ratio of heat produced in series and parallel combinations. (NCERT)
e: At constant V, H = (V²/R)t, so H_s/H_p = R_p/R_s = (R/2)/(2R) = 1 : 4.

q: A copper wire has diameter 0.5 mm and resistivity 1.6 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m. What will be the length of this wire to make its resistance 10 Ω? (NCERT)
e: With r = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m and A = πr² ≈ 1.963 × 10⁻⁷ m², l = R·A/ρ ≈ 122.7 m.

q: Resistance of a metal wire of length 1 m is 26 Ω at 20°C. If the diameter of the wire is 0.3 mm, what is the resistivity of the metal? (NCERT Ex 12.5)
e: Using ρ = Rπd²/(4l), ρ ≈ 1.84 × 10⁻⁶ Ω·m (matching manganese).

q: When a 12 V battery is connected across an unknown resistor, there is a current of 2.5 mA in the circuit. Find the value of resistance. (NCERT)
e: Converting 2.5 mA = 2.5 × 10⁻³ A gives R = 12 / (2.5 × 10⁻³) = 4800 Ω = 4.8 kΩ.

q: A 9 V battery is connected in series with resistors of 0.2 Ω, 0.3 Ω, 0.4 Ω, 0.5 Ω, and 12 Ω respectively. How much current would flow through the 12 Ω resistor? (NCERT)
e: Total series resistance = 13.4 Ω. Every resistor carries the same current I = 9 / 13.4 ≈ 0.67 A.

q: An electric iron consumes energy at a rate of 1 kW when operated at 220 V. Which fuse rating (3 A, 5 A, or 15 A) should be used for its safety?
e: Operating current I = 1000/220 ≈ 4.55 A; a 3 A fuse would blow immediately, while 5 A protects it properly.

q: How much energy is given to each coulomb of charge passing through a 6 V battery? (NCERT Intext)
e: Energy given per coulomb = W = V × Q = 6 × 1 = 6 J.

q: How many electrons are contained in 2 C of negative electric charge?
e: n = Q/e = 2 / (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 1.25 × 10¹⁹ electrons.

q: What is the operating resistance of a bulb rated 60 W at 120 V?
Two resistors 6 Ω and 12 Ω are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. What are the currents flowing through 6 Ω and 12 Ω respectively?
e: Both share V = 12 V: I₁ = 12/6 = 2 A and I₂ = 12/12 = 1 A.

e: A is true, while R is false because conventional current is opposite to electron flow.

Assertion (A): Outside a battery in a closed circuit, conventional current flows from the positive terminal to the negative terminal.
Reason (R): Positive charges tend to move from higher electric potential to lower electric potential.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R explains conventional current flow.

q:
Assertion (A): If a 100 W–220 V bulb and a 40 W–220 V bulb are connected in series across 220 V mains, the 40 W bulb glows brighter.
Reason (R): In series, both carry equal current; since R = V²/P is larger for the 40 W bulb, it dissipates greater I²R power.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: Both A and R are true, and R accurately explains why the lower-wattage bulb shines brighter in series.

q:
Assertion (A): Cutting a wire in half halves its electrical resistivity.
Reason (R): Resistance of a uniform wire is directly proportional to its length.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: A is false (resistance halves, resistivity remains constant), while R is true.

q:
Assertion (A): Running multiple heavy appliances from a single household socket is safe because parallel connections decrease total current.
Reason (R): Adding parallel branches lowers total resistance, increasing the total current drawn through the main supply cord and risking overloading.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
e: A is false (multi-plug heavy loads overload the socket cord), while R is true.

q: Case Study: V–I graphs (V on Y-axis, I on X-axis) for two metallic wires A and B are plotted. Line A makes 60° with the I-axis while line B makes 30°. Which wire has greater resistance?
o: Wire A (steeper V–I slope means higher resistance R_A > R_B)
e: With V on Y-axis and I on X-axis, slope = tan θ = R. Since tan 60° > tan 30°, R_A > R_B.

q: Case Study: A student connects a battery, switch, 10 Ω resistor, and rheostat in series, with a voltmeter across the 10 Ω resistor. After closing the switch, she slides the rheostat to decrease its resistance. What happens to the ammeter and voltmeter readings?
o: Total resistance falls so ammeter current rises, raising potential difference V = IR across the 10 Ω resistor
e: Reducing rheostat resistance boosts circuit current I, increasing V = I × 10 Ω on the voltmeter.

q: Case Study: Daily usage in a house includes a 2000 W heater for 2 h, four 100 W bulbs for 5 h, and a 500 W motor for 1 h. How many commercial units (kWh) are consumed in 30 days?
Case Study: A person observes a series string of 20 fairy bulbs and a room with 4 ceiling fans wired in parallel. If one bulb in the fairy string fuses, what happens?
o: All 20 bulbs in the series string go out because one broken filament opens the entire series loop
The parallel ceiling fans also stop
Only bulbs after the fused one stop
e: In series, a single break stops current everywhere in that loop, turning off all 20 bulbs.

q: Case Study: At 20°C, materials A, B, C, D have resistivities 1.6×10⁻⁸, 1.0×10⁻⁶, 2.63×10⁻⁸, and 10¹⁴ Ω·m. Which pair best suits (i) power cables and (ii) heating elements?
e: A/C (metals ~10⁻⁸ Ω·m) conduct power lines efficiently, B (~10⁻⁶ Ω·m alloy) makes heating coils, while D is an insulator.

q: Case Study: A student connects three identical bulbs in parallel across an ideal battery, each drawing 1 A (total 3 A). If one bulb fuses and opens, what happens to the battery current and brightness of the other two?
o: Main current drops from 3 A to 2 A, while the remaining two bulbs keep glowing at unchanged brightness
The remaining two bulbs turn off
e: Each parallel branch maintains full battery voltage, so each surviving bulb still draws 1 A (total = 2 A).

q: Case Study: Raman measures V and I for an incandescent filament lamp from low to high voltage and gets a curved V–I plot instead of a straight line. What is the physical reason?
o: As current rises, filament temperature climbs sharply, increasing its resistance so V/I is no longer constant
e: Rising filament temperature increases metallic resistance, violating the constant-temperature requirement of Ohm's law.

q: Case Study: Why is the top earth pin in a three-pin domestic electrical plug made both longer and thicker than the live and neutral pins?
o: Longer ensures earth connects first and disconnects last; thicker lowers resistance and prevents accidental insertion into live socket holes
e: Longer length grounds the casing before live contact; greater thickness reduces resistance and prevents wrong-hole insertion.

q: Case Study: Which arrangement of four resistors (10 Ω, 20 Ω, 30 Ω, 40 Ω) across a fixed 12 V battery will generate the MAXIMUM heat per second?
o: All four in parallel (minimum R_eq gives maximum power P = V²/R)
e: At fixed voltage V, P = V²/R_eq is maximised when R_eq is minimised—achieved by wiring all four in parallel.

q: Case Study: Instead of putting ten 10 Ω resistors in series, a student puts 5 in series in Branch A and 5 in series in Branch B, then connects Branch A and B in parallel. Find the net resistance.
e: Each branch is 5 × 10 = 50 Ω. Two 50 Ω branches in parallel give 50/2 = 25 Ω.

q: Two bulbs A (100 W, 220 V) and B (60 W, 220 V) are connected across 220 V mains first in parallel and then in series. Which glows brighter in each case?
o: A glows brighter in both cases
In parallel A (100 W) glows brighter, whereas in series B (60 W) glows brighter
B glows brighter in both cases
B in parallel and A in series
e: In parallel at 220 V, P ∝ 1/R so 100 W wins. Since R_60 > R_100, in series (same I) P = I²R makes the 60 W bulb brighter!

q: A uniform metallic wire of resistance 12 Ω is stretched to 3 times its original length while keeping its volume constant. What is its new resistance?
e: When volume stays constant and length increases n = 3 times, R' = n²R = 9 × 12 = 108 Ω.

q: Three 3 Ω resistors are connected to form a closed equilateral triangle. What is the equivalent resistance between any two vertices?
e: Across two corners, one 3 Ω side is in parallel with the other two sides in series (3+3 = 6 Ω): (3×6)/(3+6) = 2 Ω.

q: Four equal 2 Ω resistors form a closed square ABCD. What is the equivalent resistance between two diagonally opposite corners A and C?
e: Paths ABC (2+2 = 4 Ω) and ADC (2+2 = 4 Ω) sit in parallel across A and C, yielding 4/2 = 2 Ω.

q: In the same square ABCD (each side 2 Ω), what is the equivalent resistance between two adjacent corners A and B?
e: Across adjacent corners A and B, side AB (2 Ω) is in parallel with AD+DC+CB (6 Ω): (2×6)/(2+6) = 1.5 Ω.

q: V–I graphs (V on Y-axis, I on X-axis) for a metal wire at two temperatures T₁ and T₂ show a steeper slope at T₁ than at T₂. How are T₁ and T₂ related?
o: T₁ > T₂ (steeper V–I slope implies higher resistance, hence higher temperature)
e: Metallic resistance rises with temperature. Steeper V–I slope gives R₁ > R₂, meaning T₁ > T₂.

q: Reverse-axes trap: on an I–V graph (I on Y-axis, V on X-axis) for a metallic conductor, the line at temperature T₁ is steeper than at T₂. Which is true?
o: T₁ < T₂ (since I–V slope is 1/R, steeper slope means smaller resistance and lower temperature)
e: Here slope = I/V = 1/R. Steeper T₁ means smaller R₁, hence lower temperature T₁ < T₂.

q: Why does the safe fusing current of a fuse wire depend primarily on its cross-sectional radius and material rather than its length?
o: Because both heat generated (∝ l) and surface area radiating heat away (∝ l) scale linearly with length and cancel out
e: In thermal steady state, Joule heat per second (∝ l) balances surface heat loss (∝ l), cancelling length l out.

q: Three 6 Ω resistors are connected in series across a 12 V battery. If a zero-resistance copper wire is connected across the middle 6 Ω resistor (short-circuiting it), what becomes the circuit current?
o: Increases to 1.0 A (middle resistor is bypassed, leaving R_eq = 6+6 = 12 Ω)
e: A 0 Ω shunt shorts out the middle resistor completely, reducing total resistance from 18 Ω to 12 Ω and raising current to 1 A.

q: If a 100 W, 220 V bulb is accidentally connected across a 440 V power supply, how much instantaneous power will it draw before burning out?
e: At double the rated voltage (2×), power P = V²/R jumps 2² = 4 times to 400 W, overheating and burning the filament.

q: Two copper wires of equal length—one thin and one thick—are connected in SERIES across a 6 V battery. Which wire develops more heat?
o: The thin wire (higher resistance in series with equal current produces greater I²Rt heat)
e: In series, current I is identical so H ∝ R; the thinner wire has greater resistance and heats up more.

q: Now connect the same two equal-length copper wires (one thin, one thick) in PARALLEL across the 6 V battery. Which one generates more heat now?
o: The thick wire (at equal parallel voltage V, H = V²t/R is greater for the lower-resistance thick wire)
Current flows only in the thin wire
e: In parallel, voltage V is identical so H = V²t/R ∝ 1/R; the thicker wire has lower resistance, draws larger current, and produces more heat.

q: If 10²⁰ electrons cross a wire cross-section in 1 second (each carrying 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C), what is the electric current in the wire?
Four 6 Ω resistors are wired between X and Y such that two are in series in Branch 1, two are in series in Branch 2, and Branch 1 & 2 are in parallel across X–Y. Find R_XY.
e: Each series branch is 12 Ω; two 12 Ω branches in parallel give 12/2 = 6 Ω.

q: A 12 V battery feeds 2 Ω and 4 Ω in series. If a student mistakenly connects an ideal (0 Ω) ammeter in parallel across the 4 Ω resistor instead of a voltmeter, what current does the battery now deliver?
o: 6 A (the 0 Ω ammeter shorts out the 4 Ω resistor, leaving only 2 Ω)
e: The near-zero resistance ammeter short-circuits the 4 Ω resistor, dropping load resistance to 2 Ω and raising current to 12/2 = 6 A.

q: Three identical bulbs are connected in parallel to an ideal constant-voltage battery. If one bulb is switched off, what happens to the brightness of each remaining bulb and total power consumed?
o: Both shine brighter and total power rises
Brightness of each remaining bulb stays unchanged, while total power drops to 2/3
Brightness dims while total power stays equal
e: Voltage across each remaining branch stays V, keeping individual brightness constant while total power drops from 3P to 2P.

q: Now the same three identical bulbs are connected in SERIES across an ideal 12 V battery. If one bulb is short-circuited (bypassed by a copper wire across it), what happens to the brightness of the remaining two bulbs?
o: Both glow BRIGHTER (total resistance drops from 3R to 2R, raising voltage per bulb from 4 V to 6 V)
e: Bypassing one bulb reduces total resistance from 3R to 2R, increasing voltage across each remaining bulb from 4 V to 6 V so they glow brighter.

q: A heater coil of resistance R is cut into two equal halves and the two halves are connected in parallel across the same voltage supply. How does the new heating rate compare to the original rate?
e: Each half has resistance R/2; in parallel R' = R/4. At constant V, P' = V²/(R/4) = 4(V²/R) = 4× original power.

q: Using exactly two identical 2 Ω resistors, how many distinct non-zero equivalent resistances can you obtain by connecting both in the circuit?
o: 2 (4 Ω in series and 1 Ω in parallel)
e: Two resistors can only be combined in series (4 Ω) or in parallel (1 Ω), yielding 2 distinct values.

q: How many distinct equivalent resistance values can be obtained by combining ALL three 2 Ω resistors together?
o: 4 values (6 Ω, 3 Ω, 4/3 Ω, and 2/3 Ω)
e: Four distinct networks: all series (6 Ω), (2||2)+2 (3 Ω), (2+2)||2 (4/3 Ω), and all parallel (2/3 Ω).

q: If supply voltage drops by 10% across a pure resistive heating element (R constant), by approximately what percentage does its heat/power output decrease?
e: At 0.9V, power P' = (0.9)²P = 0.81P, which represents a 19% decrease in power.

q: A student measures 100 J of heat produced in a 2 Ω resistor over 2 seconds. What potential difference V was applied across the resistor?
A 2 V cell supplies a steady current of 0.5 A to a circuit for 1 minute. How much total electrical energy is delivered by the cell?
e: Electrical energy E = V × I × t = 2 × 0.5 × 60 = 60 J.

q: Two heating coils A and B have the same material and thickness, but coil A is twice as long as coil B. When connected in parallel to a battery, what is the ratio of heat produced H_A : H_B?
e: R_A = 2R_B. In parallel at constant voltage V, H ∝ 1/R so H_A : H_B = 1 : 2.

q: Coil A boils a fixed amount of water in 10 min alone, and Coil B boils the same water in 15 min alone across the same supply. How long will it take if both coils are switched ON together in parallel?
e: In parallel, heating powers add (P = P₁+P₂), so 1/t = 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6 => t = 6 minutes.

q: If the same two heater coils (taking 10 min and 15 min individually) are connected in SERIES across the same supply, how long will they take to boil the same water?
e: In series, resistances add (R_s = R_A + R_B), and for fixed V and energy E = V²t/R, time scales with R: t_s = 10 + 15 = 25 minutes.

q: Three appliances drawing 1 A, 2 A, and 3 A individually from a 220 V supply are operated together in parallel. What is the effective total resistance of the combined load?
e: Total parallel current I = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 A, giving R_eq = 220/6 ≈ 36.67 Ω.

q: Why can connecting a thick copper bar directly across a 12 V battery cause extreme heating and sparking almost instantly?
o: Near-zero external resistance sends current I = V/R skyrocketing, generating huge I²Rt heat instantaneously
e: Short-circuiting cuts resistance to near zero, spiking current drastically and causing intense I²R heating.

q:
Evaluate these 3 statements:
1. For the same material and length, a thick wire has lower resistance than a thin wire.
2. Both thick and thin wires of the same material have equal resistivity at the same temperature.
3. In series combination, voltage stays identical while current splits across resistors.
Which statements are TRUE?
e: Statements 1 and 2 are true; statement 3 is false (it swaps series and parallel rules).

q: Why do standard domestic electrical installations separate circuits into 5 A lighting lines and 15 A power lines?
o: So the 15 A line supplies 440 V
High-power appliances draw heavy currents requiring thicker low-resistance copper cables and a 15 A fuse to avoid overheating/tripping
e: Both circuits operate at 220 V AC, but heavy appliances draw much higher currents needing thicker cables and 15 A protection.
